text: Before data trains a model, two questions need answers: where did it actually come from, and did anyone agree to this specific use?

Provenance is the documented history of a piece of data. For training data, that means more than which database it came from — was it collected directly from the people it describes, purchased from a broker, scraped from the web, or generated by another AI system? "We're not sure" is itself a governance finding.

Consent asks whether people actually agreed to this specific use, not just whether it's technically legal. Terms of service language agreed to years ago, for a different purpose, doesn't mean someone anticipated their data training a model that decides things about other people. Consent done well is specific, not boilerplate.

Internally collected data has the clearest provenance but still needs a consent check. Licensed third-party data shifts the question to the license terms. Public or scraped data has the murkiest provenance — publicly visible isn't the same as available for any use. Another AI system's output raises its own license question.

That phrase used to be treated as sufficient and increasingly isn't. A governed organization documents the actual source, collection method, license or consent basis, and who approved it — before training starts, not after the model's already live.
